title: Priority 5: Strengthen the pull of career-connected pathways
author: Michael B. Horn, Angela Jackson, Danny Curtis and Mallory Dwinal-Palisch
summary: This is the final paper in a six-part state policy playbook from the Clayton Christensen Institute on building integrated education-to-career systems, here covering how states can create demand so that career-connected pathways become the norm. The authors argue that building pathways and removing structural barriers is not enough; students, families and employers must also choose them, so policy must make their value clear and lower the risk of participating. Three recommendations follow: reduce employer liability barriers, expand access to career guidance, and help students show skills that employers can see. Each is analysed through business model theory and a Chesterton's Fence consideration, then illustrated with a state case: Utah's House Bill 555 on youth apprentice liability, Maryland's Career Counseling Program, and the Alabama Talent Triad skills marketplace. Each section ends with takeaways for other states, stressing that protections for students should be preserved while responsibility and signals are redesigned.
points: Career-connected pathways only scale when students, families and employers all choose them, so states must act as a magnet by making pathways easier to understand, less risky and more rewarding.

Utah shifted workers' compensation and risk coverage for approved student workers onto the state Risk Management Fund, preserving protections while removing an employer deterrent, and added 53 programs in 2025.

Maryland requires school districts, community colleges and workforce boards to partner on career counseling and gives every student a six-year academic and career plan, reaching about 370 counselors statewide.

Alabama's Talent Triad shows that a shared skills ontology, credential registry and learning and employment records only work if employers describe jobs more precisely and providers tie credentials to demonstrated competence.

Each recommendation carries a Chesterton's Fence warning, such as safeguarding learner privacy and avoiding loose skills translations, so reform improves incentives without discarding the reasons existing rules exist.
quotes: Career-connected programs will only succeed at scale if students, families, and employers choose them. That means states must do more than build pathways and remove structural barriers. They must also strengthen demand by making the value clear and reducing the risks of participation.

In this role, policy acts like a magnet, attracting students, families, and employers to career-connected learning programs by making these opportunities easier to understand, less risky to pursue, and more likely to deliver valuable outcomes.

While some employers may have their doubts about the value of the model, that is not always the challenge. It is often the case that the perceived legal and financial downside outweighs the expected upside.
The goal is not deregulation, but a smarter allocation of risk that protects students while encouraging participation.

School advising systems were built primarily to support college admissions and often struggle even to fulfill that role. Counselors frequently carry high caseloads, have limited access to labor-market information, and lack the time or expertise to help students evaluate newer options such as apprenticeship, short-term credentials, and pathways that combine education with work.

Generic labels like “critical thinking” are too vague. For skills matching to work, providers and employers will need to define skills with greater precision and in the context in which they are used.
In 2025 alone, the state added 53 new programs and 23 new occupations. Its pipeline of employer-led programs has grown to serve more than 2,300 youth participants.
The goal is not simply to share more information or translate everything into a common skills language as quickly as possible. It is to build trusted signaling infrastructure.
